bib.title: Chapter 10. Operational Reinforcement Learning (in Reinforcement Learning: Industrial Applications of Intelligent Agents)

question: How do you take an RL proof of concept into production: implementation (frameworks, scaling, evaluation) and deployment (architecture, tooling, safety, security, ethics)?
contributions: First attempt (per the author) to collate operational RL knowledge in one place
Review of RL frameworks, scaling architectures, evaluation measures, deployment architecture, tooling, safe/secure/ethical RL

results.claim: Espeholt et al. measured the cost of one billion frames: IMPALA vs SEED on DeepMind Lab.
results.setup: 1 billion frames, one run, DeepMind Lab; IMPALA then SEED
results.quote: found that the total cost for a single run (one billion frames) was $236 and $54 for DeepMind Lab and $899 and $369 for Google Research Football , respectively.

results.claim: Same comparison on Google Research Football.
results.setup: 1 billion frames, one run, Google Research Football

results.claim: GPT-3 from-scratch training cost estimate at cloud list prices.

results.quote: would cost in the range of $10 million to train from scratch

results.claim: Colas et al.: at least 15 reruns needed to show SAC beats TD3 on Half-Cheetah-v2.
results.setup: TD3 vs SAC, Half-Cheetah-v2; Welch's t-test most robust for small samples
results.quote: they need to rerun each training at least 15 times to get statistically significant evidence that SAC is better than TD3

results.quote: A3C obtained comparable results to Gorila in one-eighth of the time (1 day)
results.note: Better results in about half the time (4 days).

results.claim: Gorila was over 20 times faster in wall-clock than DQN alone on Atari.
results.quote: led to superior performance over 20 times faster (wall-clock time) than DQN alone

results.setup: Atari, single machine, one GPU, many actors
results.quote: comparable results to A3C in one-eighth of the time (again!) creating efficient policies for many Atari games in about 12 hours

results.claim: DD-PPO scaled almost linearly up to 256 workers/GPUs.
results.setup: 3D navigation, synchronous distributed PPO with preemptive straggler cutoff
results.quote: increasing the number of workers almost linearly, tested up to 256 workers/GPUs

results.quote: But these scores were trained on 16 times the number of CPUs (256 versus 16 for A3C)

results.claim: SEED trains in roughly half the time of IMPALA under similar conditions.
results.quote: slightly faster training times (approximately half the time under similar conditions)

results.claim: IMPALA is an order of magnitude faster than A3C, tested with 8 GPUs.
results.setup: IMPALA multi-learner, 8 GPUs in their experiments
results.quote: improves training speed by an order of magnitude compared to A3C

results.claim: Symantec 2019: share of targeted hacks by cause.
results.setup: Symantec Internet Security Threat Report 2019; 2% web server exploits, 1% data storage exploits
results.quote: a whopping 65% of all targeted hacks were caused by phishing, 23% by unpatched software, and 5% by bogus software updates

results.claim: Author's unsupported estimate that RL products need orders of magnitude more compute than typical software.
results.quote: I am being intentionally vague, because I don't have any hard facts to support this.

limits: Author states there is little prior work on operational RL; much is extrapolated from software/ML practice and his own consulting experience (Winder Research).
Scaling comparisons come from toy environments (Atari, DeepMind Lab, Google Research Football); author says you must test on your own problem.
Ape-X comparison confounded by 16x CPUs; author says unclear whether performance differs at equal CPUs.
Author declines to review specific frameworks and tools because they date quickly (points to book website).
Predates LLM RL (2020); no LLM post-training content. Stated costs (GPT-3 $10M, cloud list prices) are 2020 figures.
No unified method of computing regret for any problem; formally constrained RL only works on toy examples; safe RL called an open problem.
practices: Weigh RL frameworks on abstractions, simplicity, observability, scalability, minimal dependencies, documentation, included/ancillary algorithms, support, commercial offerings (Frameworks).
Constrain scope early (simplify problem, use simulations, shrink models), then scale; feedback cycle time is the key development metric (Scaling RL).
Keep actors/learners close, ideally on one machine, since communication and synchronisation are bottlenecks (Single-machine training).
Report policy performance in problem-domain units; consider removing discounting for the final measure; use median/percentile when rewards are sparse (Policy performance measures).
Measure learning speed as speed of convergence to near-optimality, using environment steps, wall-clock, training steps, or compute time as fits the goal (Policy performance measures).
Visualise policy comparisons before testing; choose statistical tests knowing assumptions (Welch's t-test for small samples); tests fail silently (Statistical policy comparisons).

Verify two runs with the same seed give identical results; set seeds in Python, NumPy, Gym, DL framework, RL framework, replay buffer; then repeat with different seeds (Statistical policy comparisons).
Run a pilot study to estimate standard deviation, then compute the number of trials needed (Colas et al.) (Statistical policy comparisons).
Perturb states, models and actions adversarially to test robustness (Statistical policy comparisons).
Use the behavior suite for generic algorithm evaluation; domain benchmarks only when your problem matches (Algorithm/Problem-specific measures).
Prioritise by phase: flexibility and speed in development, provenance in hardening, state preservation and monitoring in production (Goals).
Get the basics right before automation; use the hierarchy of needs (Table 10-1) to decide how much automation is worth it (Hierarchy of needs).
Use abstractions as needed: serving interface, log, parameter server, policy servers, replay buffers, actors/critics, learning (same code as serving), data augmentation (Architecture).
Build core competencies, buy the rest, or adapt open source to 80% (Build versus buy).
Keep a dedicated log for Markov state changes; log data shapes; summarise data into metrics rather than text logs; use a correlation identifier to trace trajectories (Logging and tracing).
Unit-test incoming data against a schema (CI/CD only covers static artifacts) (CI/CD).
Track experiments in an external system and run them in parallel; TensorBoard does not scale well (Experiment tracking).
Use model-based hyperparameter tuning such as Optuna with care: it may stop slow starters early (Hyperparameter tuning).
Roll out agents by canary (with stickiness), shadowing, bandit A/B, or ensembles (Deploying multiple agents).
Stay as close to never updating the production policy as possible; make deployments stateless and immutable, treating policy updates as new deployments (Deploying policies).
Safe RL: constrained optimisation, reward penalties, imitation/inverse RL, external safe-set filters, abort-and-reset controllers; none guarantees safety during learning (Safe RL).
Secure RL: fix basics first (access control, MFA, open ports), then data integrity monitoring, rate limiting; weigh mitigation against probability of attack (Secure RL).
Ethics: ask the listed questions (bias, personal impact, climate, unintended use, nefarious use, legality, human rights, justification, performance misinformation) during development (Ethical RL).

terms.definition: a measure of how well the policy solves your problem
measures how fast you can train an agent to yield an optimal policy
the total difference between the reward if an agent was behaving optimally in hindsight and the actual reward obtained over all time
count how many times the policy needs to be updated to become optimal, during training
specify what you expect incoming data to look like in the form of a schema and test that it conforms
Route a certain proportion of users to a new agent, altered over time, with stickiness
Running other agents hidden in the background, on real data, but not serving the results to users
learn a policy that maximizes rewards while operating within predefined safety constraints
attacker alters or manipulates the training data to produce a known result
